subtopics.title: what AI is
subtopics.teaching: Artificial intelligence refers to computer systems designed to perform tasks involving capabilities such as pattern recognition, prediction, language processing or decision support.
subtopics.worked_example: A recommendation system can rank items using patterns in user behaviour without having human-like understanding.
subtopics.pitfall: AI output is not automatically evidence of consciousness or human reasoning.
subtopics.mastery: Identify AI systems by the task they perform and distinguish automated pattern processing from human intelligence.

subtopics.title: AI history
subtopics.teaching: AI has developed through multiple periods of research, including symbolic methods, expert systems, statistical learning and modern neural-network approaches.
subtopics.worked_example: Modern machine learning builds on decades of earlier work rather than appearing suddenly with generative AI.
subtopics.pitfall: A technology being newly popular does not mean its underlying research is entirely new.
subtopics.mastery: Place major AI developments in broad historical sequence and explain their significance.

subtopics.title: machine learning concepts
subtopics.teaching: Machine learning systems learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions instead of requiring every rule to be explicitly programmed.
subtopics.worked_example: A classifier trained on labelled images can learn patterns associated with different categories.
subtopics.pitfall: A model can fail when its training data does not represent the situations encountered after deployment.
subtopics.mastery: Explain training, inference, features, labels and basic model limitations.

subtopics.title: models and data
subtopics.teaching: An AI model is a learned computational representation, while data provides examples or information used during training, validation or inference.
subtopics.worked_example: Changing the training data can change a model's learned behaviour even when the model architecture remains the same.
subtopics.pitfall: More data is not automatically better if it is inaccurate, duplicated or unrepresentative.
subtopics.mastery: Explain how data and models interact and why data quality matters.

subtopics.title: AI applications
subtopics.teaching: AI applications include recommendation, speech recognition, computer vision, language processing, forecasting and decision support.
subtopics.worked_example: A speech-to-text system converts spoken language into text by processing audio patterns.
subtopics.pitfall: Calling every automated program AI can obscure the distinction between simple rules and learned systems.
subtopics.mastery: Identify appropriate AI applications and explain what task the system performs.

subtopics.title: data types
subtopics.teaching: Data can be represented as numbers, text, categories, images, audio, video and other structured or unstructured forms.
subtopics.worked_example: A student's age is numeric data, while a course category may be categorical data; each requires appropriate handling.
subtopics.pitfall: Treating every value as the same type can produce invalid analysis.
subtopics.mastery: Classify common data types and select suitable representations.

subtopics.title: patterns
subtopics.teaching: Pattern recognition identifies regularities or relationships in data that may support prediction, classification or explanation.
subtopics.worked_example: If sales repeatedly increase during a particular season, the pattern may be useful for forecasting but does not prove the season is the only cause.
subtopics.pitfall: A correlation or repeated pattern does not automatically establish causation.
subtopics.mastery: Identify meaningful patterns and distinguish observation from causal explanation.

subtopics.title: algorithms
subtopics.teaching: An algorithm is a finite sequence of precise operations for transforming inputs into outputs or solving a problem.
subtopics.worked_example: A sorting algorithm receives a collection of values and produces them in a defined order according to its comparison rules.
subtopics.pitfall: An algorithm must handle valid input cases rather than only the example used to explain it.
subtopics.mastery: Describe, trace and compare simple algorithms using clear inputs and outputs.

subtopics.title: training data
subtopics.teaching: Training data provides examples from which a machine-learning model learns patterns; its quality affects model behaviour.
subtopics.worked_example: If a face-recognition dataset underrepresents certain groups, performance may differ across those groups.
subtopics.pitfall: A large dataset can still be biased or poorly labelled.
subtopics.mastery: Evaluate training data for relevance, quality, representation and labelling.

subtopics.title: evaluation
subtopics.teaching: Model evaluation measures how well a system performs against defined criteria on data appropriate for testing.
subtopics.worked_example: A classification model can be evaluated using held-out examples rather than only the data used for training.
subtopics.pitfall: High training accuracy does not guarantee strong performance on unseen cases.
subtopics.mastery: Explain why separate evaluation data and suitable metrics are important.

subtopics.title: text generation
subtopics.teaching: Text-generation systems produce sequences of language based on patterns learned from training data and the current input context.
subtopics.worked_example: A language model can draft a summary from supplied notes, but the draft should be checked against the source material.
subtopics.pitfall: Fluent sentences can contain incorrect facts or unsupported claims.
subtopics.mastery: Use generated text as an assistive output and verify important information.

subtopics.title: image generation
subtopics.teaching: Image-generation systems create images from learned patterns conditioned on prompts or other inputs.
subtopics.worked_example: A prompt describing a classroom scene can guide a generative system toward relevant objects and composition.
subtopics.pitfall: Generated images may contain visual inaccuracies, ambiguous text or unintended details.
subtopics.mastery: Evaluate generated images for factual, visual and contextual accuracy.

subtopics.title: multimodal systems
subtopics.teaching: Multimodal systems process or generate more than one type of information, such as text, images, audio or video.
subtopics.worked_example: A system can receive an image and a text question, then produce a textual explanation based on both inputs.
subtopics.pitfall: Supporting multiple modalities does not guarantee correct interpretation of every modality.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the inputs and outputs of a multimodal system and its limitations.

subtopics.title: prompt concepts
subtopics.teaching: A prompt specifies an instruction, context, constraints or desired output that guides a generative AI system.
subtopics.worked_example: A prompt requesting a comparison with a specified audience, format and evidence requirement is more constrained than a vague request for 'tell me about it'.
subtopics.pitfall: Adding instructions cannot guarantee factual correctness.
subtopics.mastery: Construct clear prompts with relevant context, constraints and output requirements.

subtopics.title: limitations
subtopics.teaching: Generative AI can hallucinate, reflect training-data biases, misunderstand ambiguous instructions and produce inconsistent outputs.
subtopics.worked_example: Two prompts asking the same factual question can produce different wording or even different claims, so important answers require verification.
subtopics.pitfall: Confident language is not proof of correctness.
subtopics.mastery: Identify common generative-AI failure modes and apply verification and human review.

subtopics.title: sensors
subtopics.teaching: Sensors detect physical or environmental information such as distance, light, temperature, pressure or motion and convert it into usable signals.
subtopics.worked_example: A robot using a distance sensor can detect an obstacle and trigger a change in movement.
subtopics.pitfall: A sensor measures a property; it does not by itself decide what action should follow.
subtopics.mastery: Match common sensors with the information they can measure.

subtopics.title: actuators
subtopics.teaching: Actuators convert control signals into physical action, such as movement, rotation, gripping or switching.
subtopics.worked_example: A motor can act as an actuator that turns an electrical control signal into mechanical motion.
subtopics.pitfall: A sensor and actuator perform different roles in a control system.
subtopics.mastery: Distinguish sensing from actuation and explain how they work together.

subtopics.title: control
subtopics.teaching: Control systems use inputs, decision logic and outputs to regulate behaviour toward a desired state.
subtopics.worked_example: A thermostat senses temperature and controls heating based on a chosen set point.
subtopics.pitfall: Changing the threshold changes when the actuator responds.
subtopics.mastery: Trace a simple feedback or control loop from sensor input to action.

subtopics.title: autonomous systems
subtopics.teaching: An autonomous system performs some actions with limited direct human control by sensing conditions and selecting responses according to programmed or learned rules.
subtopics.worked_example: A robot vacuum can map or sense its environment and adjust movement without a person steering every turn.
subtopics.pitfall: Autonomous does not mean independent of all human design, goals or constraints.
subtopics.mastery: Identify sensing, decision and action components in autonomous systems.

subtopics.title: real-world automation
subtopics.teaching: Real-world automation combines software, hardware, data and procedures to perform repeatable tasks with limited manual intervention.
subtopics.worked_example: An automated warehouse system can scan items, update inventory and route packages while using sensors and control logic.
subtopics.pitfall: Automating a flawed process can reproduce errors at greater speed and scale.
subtopics.mastery: Evaluate where automation is useful and where human checks remain necessary.
